It starts in the spring of 1963,
in Birmingham, Alabama.
Black residents there were protesting segregation,
and Martin Luther King was one of the leaders.
That spring the city saw violence,
including a bombing at the Gaston Motel,
and a Library of Congress
photograph shows the damage.
Faced with the protests, President John F.
Kennedy decided to back a new civil rights law.
On 11 June 1963, he went on radio
and television to explain why.
That same day, National
Guard troops had been needed
to admit two Black students
to the University of Alabama.
He told the country that a Black baby born
in America that day had about half the chance
of finishing high school that a white
baby born the same day had.
Then he named the problem.
Eight days later, he sent his proposal to Congress.
The National Archives notes
that the message stressed how segregation
hurt the nation's standing in the world,
in the middle of the Cold War.
Civil rights leaders wanted to show Washington
how many people stood behind the bill.
A. Philip Randolph, a veteran labor leader,
had been calling for a march on Washington,
and in May King joined that call.
Its official name was the March
on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.
It demanded a strong civil rights bill,
protection of the vote, school desegregation,
and a federal jobs program.
The date was 28 August, eleven
weeks after Kennedy's speech.
On 28 August 1963, people poured into Washington
from all over the country, many of them by bus.
The National Archives says
hundreds of thousands came.
They gathered at the Lincoln Memorial.
History.com reports that the leaders
chose it, rather than the Capitol,
so members of Congress would not feel under siege.
A film crew from the United States
Information Agency recorded the day,
and the film still has its sound.
Singing ran through the program,
and so did speeches.
Another speaker talked about how
America would look from abroad.
Then a speaker singled out King.
A minister's prayer asked God
to bless the United States.
According to John Lewis's memoir,
his own speech was toned down that day
after objections from other leaders.
According to Clarence B. Jones,
King's lawyer and adviser,
A. Philip Randolph argued that King should speak
last, because most people were coming to hear him.
Jones gave that account in a 2013 oral
history for the Library of Congress.
When King reached the microphones
at the Lincoln Memorial,
he began by reading from his prepared text.
By his own account, King had finished
that text around three thirty that morning.
A typescript had already gone to the press.
Jones says he drafted the first
six or seven paragraphs,
including the passage about
a promissory note and insufficient funds.
Here is King delivering that passage.
Then, Jones says, the singer Mahalia
Jackson, who had performed earlier,
called out to King to tell them about the dream.
Here is Jones telling it himself.
Jones says King moved his text to the side

After the march, King and the other leaders went
to the White House to meet President Kennedy.
The next day, James Reston
wrote in the New York Times
that King had touched all the themes of the day,
only better than anybody else.
Inside the FBI, a quiet fight
had been going on for weeks.
Hoover had already written on an FBI memo,
back in 1962, that King was no good.
A Senate committee, led by Frank Church,
later published the paper trail.
In the week before the march,
the bureau's domestic intelligence division sent
Director J. Edgar Hoover a sixty seven page study.
It found that the Communist Party had mostly
failed to win influence among Black Americans.
Hoover disliked that answer.
He wrote across it that it reminded him
of memos he had received about Fidel Castro,
and that time had proved those analysts wrong.
William Sullivan, who ran that division, later told
the Senate that his men feared for their jobs,
and wanted a new memo to get out of trouble.
He wrote it on 30 August 1963,
two days after the speech.
In it, Sullivan said that after King's
powerful demagogic speech,
King stood head and shoulders above
all other Negro leaders put together
in influencing great masses of people.
He said the bureau must now mark King as the most
dangerous Negro of the future in this nation.
That is the shock this story can prove.
In 1975, Sullivan told the Senate that he put
in that memo what Hoover wanted to hear.
Sullivan also told the committee
that writing it meant a lot
of nonsense that he and his men
did not really believe in.
They either did that, he said,
or they would be finished.
Either way, the memo shows
how the bureau read the speech.
On 16 September, Sullivan asked
for more aggressive coverage.
Hoover refused, asking how
he could switch so quickly,
when only weeks before he had called
Communist influence ineffective.
In October, Attorney General Robert Kennedy
approved FBI wiretaps on King's home and offices.
The committee could not establish why he said
yes after refusing the same request in July.
In December, senior FBI officials met
to plan ways to neutralize King's influence.
Days later, Time magazine
named King Man of the Year,
and Hoover said they had to dig deep
in the garbage to come up with that one.
Meanwhile the law moved.
President Johnson signed
the Civil Rights Act on 2 July 1964.
King won the Nobel Peace Prize that year.
He received it in Oslo on 10 December 1964.
In 1965, marchers walked from Selma
to Montgomery for the right to vote,
and the Voting Rights Act was signed on 6 August.
On 4 April 1968, King was shot
dead in Memphis, Tennessee.
He was 39.
